raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils, most commonly immunoglobulin light chain (AL) amyloid or transthyretin amyloid (ATTR) [1,2]. Accurate amyloid typing is fundamental, because AL cardiac amyloidosis is a hematologic emergency, whereas ATTR cardiomyopathy is treated by stabilizing or reducing transthyretin [3]. Clinically, the disease should be considered in older adults with heart failure and increased ventricular wall thickness, unexplained low-flow aortic stenosis, bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, neuropathy, nephrotic-range proteinuria, macroglossia, periorbital purpura, disproportionate biomarker elevation, or discordance between low electrocardiographic voltage and echocardiographic hypertrophy [4].

The major cardiac phenotypes are AL amyloidosis, wild-type ATTR, and hereditary variant ATTR. AL amyloidosis often progresses rapidly because circulating light chains are directly cardiotoxic in addition to forming fibrils; untreated advanced cardiac involvement carries a poor prognosis [5]. Wild-type ATTR, historically called senile systemic amyloidosis, predominantly affects older men and is increasingly recognized as an important cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction [6]. ATTR is also enriched among older patients referred for transcatheter aortic valve replacement, where coexistent amyloid may contribute to persistent symptoms after valve intervention [7]. Hereditary ATTR reflects pathogenic TTR variants; the Val122Ile variant is particularly important in people of African ancestry and is associated with late-onset cardiomyopathy [8].

Diagnosis has shifted from late recognition by endomyocardial biopsy to earlier, algorithmic testing [9,10]. Initial evaluation should exclude AL amyloidosis with serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation; tissue confirmation and amyloid typing remain mandatory when monoclonal gammopathy is present or scintigraphy is equivocal. Laser microdissection with mass spectrometry has become a reference standard for amyloid typing because immunohistochemistry can misclassify deposits [11]. Bone-avid tracer scintigraphy with technetium-labeled pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP is highly informative for ATTR. Seminal DPD and pyrophosphate studies showed strong uptake in ATTR compared with AL amyloid [12,13], and a multicenter analysis established that grade 2–3 myocardial uptake plus absence of a monoclonal protein can diagnose ATTR cardiomyopathy noninvasively [14].

Echocardiography typically shows increased biventricular wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, valvular thickening, restrictive filling, and impaired longitudinal function. Relative apical sparing of longitudinal strain is a useful clue, although not fully specific [15]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance adds tissue characterization: diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal nulling, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume support amyloid infiltration and provide prognostic information [16,17]. Cardiac biomarkers are central in AL amyloidosis; troponin and NT-proBNP staging identifies steep mortality gradients [18], and incorporation of the involved–uninvolved free light-chain difference further refines risk [19]. ATTR-specific staging systems using NT-proBNP, troponin, and renal function stratify survival in both wild-type and hereditary disease [20,21].

Management combines heart-failure care, arrhythmia prevention, disease-modifying therapy, and multidisciplinary monitoring. Conventional heart-failure drugs are often poorly tolerated because stroke volume is fixed and autonomic dysfunction is common; cautious loop diuresis remains the mainstay for congestion. Atrial fibrillation is frequent and poorly tolerated. Intracardiac thrombus can occur even in sinus rhythm, supporting a low threshold for anticoagulation when atrial mechanical dysfunction or atrial arrhythmia is present [22]. Pacemakers are used for conduction disease, whereas implantable defibrillator decisions should be individualized because electromechanical dissociation may limit benefit.

For AL amyloidosis, treatment targets the plasma-cell clone and aims for rapid, deep hematologic response, since cardiac biomarker improvement follows suppression of toxic light chains [23,24]. Bortezomib-based regimens accelerated responses and became a backbone of therapy [25]. The ANDROMEDA trial established daratumumab plus cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone as a highly effective first-line regimen, improving hematologic and organ responses compared with chemotherapy alone [26]. Selected patients may benefit from autologous stem-cell transplantation, but advanced cardiac involvement markedly increases treatment risk.

For ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis changed the natural history by reducing mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization while slowing functional decline [27]. Gene-silencing therapies developed for hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy, including patisiran and inotersen, reduce hepatic transthyretin production and have shown favorable cardiac signals, supporting the broader strategy of TTR knockdown [28,29]. New stabilizers such as acoramidis/AG10 were designed to more completely stabilize the transthyretin tetramer and illustrate continuing therapeutic expansion [30]. Earlier diagnosis is now the central challenge: many patients are still recognized after irreversible myocardial remodeling. A practical approach—screening for monoclonal protein, using bone scintigraphy appropriately, confirming type when needed, and promptly initiating clone-directed or ATTR-directed therapy—offers the best opportunity to improve outcomes.
